label: NSFG 1995 and 2006–2010

explanation: The original authors (OAs) compared women who were interviewed by the National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG) in 1995 with women who were interviewed in 2006–2010. These are the two cohorts of the claim, and every specification of the curve compares them.

label: NSFG 2002 and 2006–2010
reason: Cohorts about seven years apart, which SCORE compared in its reproduction: a different question.
phrase: in the NSFG of 2002 and of 2006–2010
estimates: The change between unions begun in 1997–2002 and unions begun in 2005–2010.
explanation: The file that SCORE built held five surveys, and its reproduction compared 2002 with 2006–2010 rather than 1995 with 2006–2010. Cohorts that began their unions about seven years apart answer a narrower question than the paper, which spans fifteen years. At the reference settings the decline is smaller and falls short of significance at the 5% level.

label: NSFG 1995 and 2011–2015
reason: A later cohort from new surveys: a replication of the trend rather than the comparison of the paper.
phrase: in the NSFG of 1995 and of 2011–2015
estimates: The change between unions begun in 1990–1995 and those begun in the five years before the 2011–2013 and 2013–2015 surveys.
explanation: The two later surveys extend the comparison by about five years. Fitting the reference specification to them asks whether the decline holds in data that the OAs did not use, which is replication rather than robustness, so the case teaches it with the replication.

label: NSFG 2002 and 2011–2015
reason: The surveys of the SCORE replication: new cohorts, and so a replication of the trend.
phrase: in the NSFG of 2002 and of 2011–2015
estimates: The change between unions begun in 1997–2002 and those begun in the five years before the 2011–2013 and 2013–2015 surveys.
explanation: SCORE tested the paper on these surveys, which it treated as new data. Its test concerned the interaction of some college and period, but the same surveys also show whether cohabitors of the later cohort married less, which the course fits as part of the replication.

label: NSFG 2006–2010 and 2011–2015
reason: Whether the decline went on after 2010: a question about a later period.
phrase: in the NSFG of 2006–2010 and of 2011–2015
estimates: The change between unions begun in 2005–2010 and those begun in the five years before the 2011–2013 and 2013–2015 surveys.
explanation: A comparison of the later cohort of the paper with the cohorts that followed it asks whether the decline continued, which the claim does not say. At the reference settings it points the same way but falls short of significance at the 5% level.

label: Trend over five surveys
reason: A linear trend over five surveys asks whether marriage declined steadily, which is more than the claim says.
phrase: across the five NSFG surveys from 1995 to 2013–2015, as a linear trend
estimates: The average change per year in the chance of marrying over five cohabiting cohorts.
explanation: Two Multi100 analysts used all five surveys of the file that they were given and estimated a trend over time. A steady decline is a stronger claim than the one of the paper, which compares two cohorts, and a line through five surveys can hide a change that happened between two of them.

label: Window of the paper
reason: The cohorts of the paper: unions begun in 1990–1995 against unions begun in 2005–2010.
phrase: unions begun in 1990–1995 against unions begun in 2005–2010
estimates: The change between first cohabitations that began in the five years before the 1995 interview and those that began in 2005 or later before the 2006–2010 interview.
explanation: Both surveys ask women when each union began, and the paper keeps the unions that began no more than five years before the interview. In the 2006–2010 survey it keeps only those that began in 2005 or later, so that the later cohort is as recent as the survey allows. This is the comparison of the reference specification.

label: Same window in both
reason: The same rule in both surveys: every union begun in the five years before the interview.
phrase: unions begun in the five years before each interview
estimates: The change between the two cohorts when the later one also takes in the unions that began from 2001, which the five-year rule allows for women who were interviewed in 2006.
explanation: The paper applies its five-year rule to both surveys and adds a second restriction, to 2005 or later, in the later one. Applying one rule to both makes the two cohorts alike in how they were selected, at the cost of a later cohort that reaches back to 2001 and so sits closer to the earlier one. Both readings answer whether later cohabitors marry less; the second gives a smaller decline.

label: All observed months
reason: Every month in which a union was observed, up to five years, as in the models of the paper.
phrase: in any month of the first five years of the union
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying over the whole time in which the unions were observed, at most five years.
explanation: The person-months of the paper follow each union from the month in which the couple moved in until they married, separated or were interviewed, which is at most five years later. The coefficient of the later cohort averages the difference over all those months.

label: First three years
reason: The first three years of each union, the time frame of the life table that the paper quotes.
phrase: in any month of the first three years of the union
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying within the first three years of the union.
explanation: The paper describes the decline with a life table that runs to the end of the third year, in which 41% of the earlier and 24% of the later cohort had married. Stopping the person-months at 36 months asks the same question for the years in which most cohabitors who marry do so, and in which both cohorts are observed in large numbers.

label: Marriage to the partner
reason: The cohabiting couple married each other, the transition that the claim names.
phrase: the chance that a cohabiting couple marries
estimates: Whether the couple who live together marry each other, in each month in which they are still together and unmarried.
explanation: The NSFG records how each first cohabitation ended: still intact at the interview, a marriage of the partners, or a separation. The claim is about the second of these, and the paper models it as a transition that can happen in any month of the union.

label: Married by the interview
reason: The share of unions that had become a marriage by the interview ignores how long each union was observed.
phrase: the share of unions that had become a marriage by the interview
estimates: The share of unions that had ended in marriage by the time of the interview, whatever their length.
explanation: Three Multi100 analysts kept one row per woman, the last month of her union, and compared the shares that had married. A union that began a month before the interview has had little time to become a marriage, so this share depends on when the unions began relative to the interview as much as on how readily cohabitors marry. The event-history model compares the unions month by month and so removes that difference.

label: Married within three years
reason: The share married within three years, from the life table, answers the question in absolute terms and is shown beside the curve.
phrase: the share of unions that become a marriage within three years
estimates: The share of unions that become a marriage within three years of moving in, with separation as the competing way out.
explanation: The life table gives this share for each cohort: 41% against 24% in the paper and 45% against 29% in the course rebuild. It describes the decline in the units that readers grasp most readily, but it cannot be adjusted for the composition of the cohorts in the way that a regression model can, so the course shows it as a display.

label: Separation
reason: The transition to separation is the other way out of cohabitation and the subject of another claim.
phrase: the chance that a cohabiting couple separates
estimates: Whether a cohabiting couple splits up, in each month in which they are still together.
explanation: The multinomial model of the paper estimates the chance of separating beside the chance of marrying. Separation became more common between the cohorts, but the claim of the case is about marriage.

label: No adjustment
reason: The change between the cohorts as they were, with only the time since the start of the union in the model.
phrase: without holding anything else constant
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying between the two cohorts of cohabitors as they were.
explanation: The claim says that cohabitors have become less likely to marry. Read as a description of two populations, it needs no adjustment: if the later cohabitors differ in age or in race-ethnicity, that is part of how the population of cohabitors changed.

label: Age at the start
reason: Holds constant the age at which the couple moved in, the strongest of the controls in the model.
phrase: for women who moved in at the same age
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying between cohabitors of the two cohorts who began their unions at the same age.
explanation: Women who move in with a partner at an older age marry sooner. Holding the age at the start constant, with its square as the paper does, compares cohabitors who are alike on that predictor, although the average age at the start was the same in both cohorts.

label: Age, race-ethnicity and education
reason: The controls of the paper without its interactions: the change for cohabitors of the same age, race-ethnicity and education.
phrase: for women of the same age at the start, race-ethnicity and education
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying between cohabitors of the two cohorts who share age at the start, race-ethnicity and education.
explanation: The paper models the marriage of cohabitors with age at the start, race-ethnicity and education, and the second Multi100 task excluded the interaction of education and period. This model leaves out both interactions of the paper, and it is the reference specification of the curve. Between the cohorts the share of Hispanic women among cohabitors almost doubled, so the adjusted change describes the decline within groups rather than across a changing population.

label: As in Model 2
reason: Model 2 of the paper adds race-ethnicity x period, so the coefficient of the later cohort is the change for non-Hispanic white women only.
phrase: for non-Hispanic white women of the same age at the start and education
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying between the cohorts among non-Hispanic white women.
explanation: The coefficient that the claim quotes, −0.683, comes from Model 2 of Table 2, which lets the change differ by race-ethnicity. In such a model the coefficient of the period is the change in the reference group, non-Hispanic white women, and not the average change of all cohabitors. The course refits it in the second part of the reproduction of Task 3.

label: As in Model 1
reason: Model 1 of the paper adds education x period, which the second Multi100 task excluded: the coefficient is the change for college graduates only.
phrase: for college graduates of the same age at the start and race-ethnicity
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying between the cohorts among women with a college degree.
explanation: The main argument of the paper is that marriage declined among cohabitors without a college degree and not among graduates. In Model 1 the coefficient of the period is the change for graduates (−0.137, not significant), and the declines of the other groups sit in the interaction terms. An analyst who read that coefficient as the answer would find no decline. The second Multi100 task excluded the interaction, which singles out the period coefficient of Model 2 as the result of the claim.

label: Length of the whole union
reason: Controlling for the total length of the union conditions on information that exists only once the union has ended.
phrase: for unions of the same total length
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying between unions of the two cohorts that lasted equally long in all.
explanation: The file that SCORE built carries the total length of each union in every one of its months, and several analysts entered it as a control. How long a union lasts depends on whether and when it ends in marriage, so holding it constant compares unions by their outcome. In an event-history model, time enters as the month since the couple moved in, which is known in every month.

label: Plans to marry
reason: Engagement at the start of the union was not asked in the 1995 survey, so it cannot be held constant across the cohorts.
phrase: for women with the same plans to marry
estimates: The difference in the monthly chance of marrying between cohabitors who were engaged, or not, when they moved in.
explanation: The second part of the paper asks whether plans to marry explain the differences by education in the later cohort. The question was not asked in 1995, so it can describe only the later cohort.

label: Survey weights
reason: The weights of each survey make the estimate describe the population of women aged 15–44, as the paper does.
phrase: weighted to the population of each survey
estimates: The change in the population of cohabiting women that each survey represents.
explanation: The NSFG samples Black and Hispanic women at higher rates than other women (and, from 2002, women aged 15–24 as well), and its weights correct for this and for nonresponse. The paper reports weighted results, and the course uses the final weight of each survey.

label: No weights
reason: Every union counts the same, as in the SCORE file and in every Multi100 analysis.
phrase: with every union counted the same
estimates: The change in the sample of cohabiting women that the two surveys interviewed.
explanation: The file that Multi100 gave the analysts carried no weights. Without them the estimate describes the sample, in which Black and Hispanic women count for more than they do in the population. Because the decline differs by race-ethnicity, leaving out the weights moves the estimate by about 0.05.

label: Women, first premarital unions
reason: Women aged 15–44 and the first cohabitation that came before any marriage, as in the paper.
phrase: among women aged 15–44 whose first cohabitation came before any marriage
estimates: The change among women of childbearing age whose first union with a partner was a cohabitation.
explanation: The paper studies the first premarital cohabitation of each woman, which the recodes of both surveys describe in the same way, and notes that later cohabitations are less stable and less likely to end in marriage, so that the restriction likely makes its estimates of the differences by education and race-ethnicity conservative. Women whose first cohabitation came after a marriage are left out.

label: Men as well
reason: The 1995 survey interviewed only women, so men cannot be compared across the cohorts.
phrase: among men and women
estimates: The change among cohabiting men and women.
explanation: The NSFG has interviewed men since 2002. A comparison with 1995 is therefore possible for women only, as the paper notes.

label: Every cohabitation
reason: Second and later cohabitations, and those after a marriage, are a different population of unions.
phrase: among all cohabitations of women aged 15–44
estimates: The change in the chance of marrying among all cohabiting unions, whatever their order.
explanation: Women who have cohabited before, or who have been married, enter later unions with different prospects of marriage. The paper keeps to first premarital unions and notes that its estimates of the differences by education and race-ethnicity are likely conservative for that reason.

label: Rebuilt from the NSFG
reason: The start, end and outcome of each union from the dates of the NSFG, which reproduce the counts of the paper exactly.
phrase: with the union histories rebuilt from the dates in the surveys
estimates: Unions whose start, end and outcome come from the recodes and dates of each survey.
explanation: The course rebuilds each first premarital cohabitation from the recodes of the two surveys (in 1995, the end of a union comes from the date of the marriage or of the separation). The rebuild finds the 929 and 1,142 unions of the paper with the same counts of marriages, separations and intact unions.

label: The SCORE file
reason: The person-month file that Multi100 gave the analysts lost most of the 1995 cohort: it holds 376 unions of 1995, only 351 of them among the 929 of the paper, with 369 separations and 4 marriages.
phrase: with the union histories of the SCORE file
estimates: The same comparison on the person-month file that SCORE built for its replication.
explanation: SCORE took the end of each 1995 union from the date on which the woman stopped living with a former partner, which exists only for unions that dissolved. Unions that became marriages, or were still intact at the interview, lost their end date and dropped out. Every analysis that compared 1995 with 2006–2010 on that file found marriage becoming more common, the opposite of the claim, and with the 1995 cohort rebuilt the same analyses find a decline.

label: As in Table 1
reason: Four groups with the associate degree counted as some college and the corrected coding of the GED in 2006–2010, which reproduce the shares of Table 1.
phrase: with education in four groups as in the paper
estimates: Education at the interview in four groups: less than high school, high school or GED, some college (including an associate degree), and a bachelor's degree or more.
explanation: The shares of Table 1 of the paper come out exactly when the associate degree is counted with some college and when the coding error of the 2006–2010 recode, in which some women with a GED were counted below high school, is corrected as NCHS advises.

label: As in the SCORE file
reason: The associate degree counted as college and the 2006–2010 recode as released, as in the SCORE file; the reference estimate moves by less than 0.01.
phrase: with education coded as in the SCORE file
estimates: Education at the interview with the associate degree counted as college and the 2006–2010 recode left uncorrected.
explanation: The SCORE file and the Multi100 analysts used this coding. It moves 48 of the 929 women of 1995 and 107 of the 1,142 women of 2006–2010 into another group, but education enters the curve only as a control, so the estimate of the change barely moves.

label: Left out
reason: Unions that lasted less than a month are left out, as the paper does (30 unions).
phrase: leaving out unions that lasted less than a month
estimates: The change among unions that lasted at least a month.
explanation: The paper leaves out 30 cohabitations that lasted less than a month, because so short a period of living together is ambiguous as a union. The rebuild finds 30 such unions (11 in 1995 and 19 in 2006–2010).

label: Kept
reason: Keeping the 30 unions of less than a month changes the reference estimate by about 0.02.
phrase: keeping unions that lasted less than a month
estimates: The change among all first premarital cohabitations, however short.
explanation: A union that ended in the month in which it began contributes one person-month. Keeping these unions is a check on the exclusion of the paper.

label: Person-months
reason: One row for each month in which a union could end, the discrete-time event history of the paper.
phrase: on the months in which each union could end
estimates: Monthly chances of marrying, compared between the cohorts month by month.
explanation: A discrete-time event-history model turns each union into a row for every month from the start to the marriage, the separation or the interview. Unions that are still intact at the interview contribute the months in which they were observed and are not counted as failures to marry, which is what makes the comparison fair to recent unions.

label: One row per union
reason: One row per union with its final outcome ignores how long each union was observed (three Multi100 analysts).
phrase: on one row per union with its outcome at the interview
estimates: The odds that a union had become a marriage by the interview, compared between the cohorts.
explanation: Keeping only the last month of each union treats a union that began a month before the interview like one that has run for five years. The analysts who did so controlled for the total length of the union, which brings in a variable that depends on the outcome.

label: Test of proportions on rows
reason: A test of the share of person-month rows that record a marriage ignores the time since the start and treats the months of one union as independent.
phrase: on the share of person-months that record a marriage
estimates: The crude monthly rate of marriage in each cohort, compared by a two-sample test.
explanation: One analyst compared the share of rows of the person-month file that record a marriage. On correct data this is a crude version of the monthly rate, and it points the way of the claim. Its test treats every month as an independent observation and ignores the survey design.

label: Months since the start
reason: The chance of marrying changes steadily with the time since the couple moved in, as the paper models it.
phrase: with a steady change over the months of the union
estimates: The difference between the cohorts, allowing the monthly chance of marrying to rise or fall steadily with the time since the start.
explanation: The paper controls for the duration of the union, which in a person-month model is the month since the couple moved in. A linear term lets the chance of marrying change at a constant rate over the months.

label: One step per year
reason: A separate baseline chance for each year of the union, which assumes no shape.
phrase: with a separate baseline chance for each year of the union
estimates: The difference between the cohorts, with the monthly chance of marrying free to differ from one year of the union to the next.
explanation: Dummies for the first, second, third, fourth and fifth year of the union let the baseline chance of marrying take any shape across the years. The estimate of the change between the cohorts is almost the same as with a linear term.

label: No time term
reason: Without a term for the time since the start, the model assumes that the chance of marrying is the same in every month of a union.
phrase: with the same chance in every month of the union
estimates: The difference between the cohorts in an average monthly chance of marrying that does not depend on the time since the start.
explanation: One analyst fitted the person-month model without a term for time. A constant chance is a strong assumption for unions in which marriages cluster in the first years; on these data it changes the estimate very little.

label: Multinomial logit
reason: Marriage and separation as competing ways out of the union, each against staying together: the model of the paper.
phrase: Estimated by a multinomial logit of marrying or separating against staying together
estimates: The log of the ratio of the relative chances of marrying rather than staying together in the later and the earlier cohort.
explanation: The paper fits a multinomial logistic regression to the person-months, with one equation for marrying and one for separating, both against staying together. The coefficient of the later cohort in the marriage equation is the estimate of the claim.

label: Logit
reason: The monthly chance of marriage, with a separation counted as a month without marriage that ends the union.
phrase: Estimated by a logit of marrying in the month
estimates: The log of the ratio of the odds of marrying in a month in the later and the earlier cohort.
explanation: A binary logit of marriage in each month is the simplest discrete-time hazard model. Separation ends the union, so a union contributes no months after it. With monthly chances of a few per cent, the coefficient is very close to that of the multinomial model.

label: Complementary log-log
reason: The discrete-time version of a proportional hazards model: the coefficient is the log of the ratio of the monthly rates of marriage.
phrase: Estimated by a complementary log-log model of marrying in the month
estimates: The log of the ratio of the rates of marriage in the later and the earlier cohort.
explanation: The complementary log-log link gives the discrete-time model that corresponds to a proportional hazards model in continuous time, so its coefficient is a log hazard ratio. With small monthly chances it differs little from the logit.

label: Linear probability
reason: The difference in the monthly probability of marriage in percentage points, on another scale from the curve (−1.4 points at the reference settings).
phrase: Estimated by a linear probability model of marrying in the month
estimates: The difference in the monthly probability of marrying, in percentage points.
explanation: A linear model of the monthly outcome gives the difference in probability directly. It is a useful check of the size of the change, but its coefficient is on another scale from the log ratios of the curve, so it stays off the curve.

label: Survey design
reason: Errors that take the strata and clusters of both surveys into account, as NCHS advises; they class the curve.
phrase: tested with errors that follow the design of the surveys
estimates: The uncertainty of the estimate given that the women were sampled in clusters within strata.
explanation: The NSFG samples women in clusters within strata, and its documentation asks users to estimate errors with the design variables (strata and clusters) and the weights. The course does so by linearisation, as the survey package does, with the strata and clusters of both surveys.

label: Clustered by woman
reason: Treats the months of each woman as a cluster but ignores the strata and clusters of the survey; the errors are a little smaller.
phrase: tested with errors clustered by woman
estimates: The uncertainty of the estimate given that the months of one union belong together.
explanation: Errors clustered by woman allow for the months of a union being related, but not for the clustering of women in the sample. They are stored for every specification of the curve as a check.

label: Conventional
reason: Treats every person-month as independent and ignores the survey design, which understates the error by about a quarter.
phrase: tested with conventional errors
estimates: The uncertainty of the estimate if every person-month were an independent observation.
explanation: The errors that a model reports by default ignore the weights and the clusters of the survey. Here they are about a quarter smaller than the design-based errors, which makes every test look stronger than the data allow.

label: Log scale
reason: The coefficient of the later cohort on the log scale of the model, the scale on which the paper reports −0.683.
phrase: and reported as a coefficient on the log scale
estimates: The log of the ratio of the monthly chances of marrying in the later and the earlier cohort.
explanation: Logit, multinomial and complementary log-log coefficients are all logs of ratios of monthly chances, and with chances of a few per cent a month they nearly coincide. The curve reports them on that common scale.

label: Odds or hazard ratio
reason: The exponent of the coefficient: the later cohort married at about half the monthly rate of the earlier one (0.48 at the reference settings).
phrase: and reported as a ratio
estimates: The ratio of the monthly chances of marrying in the later and the earlier cohort.
explanation: Raising e to the power of the coefficient turns it into a ratio, which most readers find easier to grasp. The curve stores it beside the coefficient.

label: Partial correlation
reason: The Multi100 conversion, from the conventional z and the number of person-months; it is small in any event-history model, because most months record no event.
phrase: and reported as a partial correlation
estimates: The partial correlation that Multi100 computed from a z statistic and the sample size.
explanation: Multi100 converted every result to a correlation, using the number of observations where a test has no degrees of freedom. In a person-month model that number counts months, almost all of which record no event, so the correlation is close to zero however large the change. Multi100 recorded 0.900 for one analyst because the conversion was applied to a regression on five points.
